title: Session-Based Authentication
subtitle: How the server remembers a signed-in user, one request to the next.
throughline: One session token: born when a user signs in, carried in a cookie, validated on every request, and finally slid forward or revoked.

chapters.title: Creating a Session
chapters.blurb: After sign-in the server mints a random token, stores only its hash, and hands the raw token back to the user.

steps.title: Creating a Session
steps.coverSubtitle: The user has proven who they are. Now the server needs a way to remember it.
steps.spoken: Authentication proves who you are once. A session is how the server keeps remembering it.
steps.displayNarration: Once a user has authenticated, the server creates a **session** so it doesn't have to re-check the password on every request.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — sessions persist authentication across requests

steps.title: A user has just signed in
steps.spoken: Our user has just signed in successfully. The app server now has to issue something the browser can present on the next request to prove it is still them.
steps.displayNarration: The **app server** has verified the credentials. It now needs to mint a **session token** the client can send back on later requests.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — a session is created after a successful sign-in

steps.title: Mint a random token
steps.spoken: First the server generates a session token: twenty random bytes from a cryptographically secure generator, encoded into a hard-to-guess string. It must be unpredictable, because anyone holding this token is treated as the user.
steps.displayNarration: The server draws **20 random bytes** from a CSPRNG — `crypto.getRandomValues()` — and encodes them (base32) into the **session token**. Unpredictability is the whole security property.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — generate a session token from at least 20 random bytes

steps.title: Hash it into a session ID
steps.spoken: The server never stores the token itself. Instead it runs the token through a fast one-way hash to derive a session ID. That hash becomes the row's primary key.
steps.displayNarration: The **session ID** is `SHA-256(token)` — a one-way hash. The raw token is never persisted, so the ID is what the database keys on.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — the session ID is the SHA-256 hash of the token

steps.title: Store only the hash
steps.spoken: The server writes one row keyed by that session ID, alongside the user's identifier and an expiry timestamp set thirty days out. Because only the hash is stored, a leaked database hands an attacker no usable tokens.
steps.displayNarration: Insert a row: `{ id: sessionId, user_id, expires_at }`, with `expires_at` set ~**30 days** ahead. Storing only the hash means a database dump yields no working tokens.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — store the session id, user id, and expiration

steps.title: Hand the raw token back
steps.spoken: Finally the server sends the raw token, not the hash, back to the user. The client keeps the token; the server keeps the hash. Neither side stores the other's secret in a usable form.
steps.displayNarration: The **raw token** is returned to the client. The split is deliberate: the client holds the token, the server holds only `SHA-256(token)`.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — return the token to the client, store the hash

steps.title: One token, two halves
steps.spoken: So a sign-in produces a random token, a stored hash of it, and a thirty-day expiry. Next we need a place for the client to keep that token safely.
steps.displayNarration: A session is a **random token** held by the client plus a **hashed row** held by the server. Next: where the browser keeps the token — the *cookie*.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — the token lives with the client, the hash with the server

chapters.title: The Session Cookie
chapters.blurb: The token rides in a cookie the browser attaches automatically, hardened by HttpOnly, SameSite, and Secure.

steps.title: The Session Cookie
steps.coverSubtitle: A cookie is just a place for the token to live — but its attributes are the security.
steps.spoken: The token needs a home in the browser. That home is a cookie, and its attributes do the defending.
steps.displayNarration: The session token is delivered and stored as an HTTP **cookie**. The cookie's *attributes* are what make it safe to use as an identity.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — store the session token in a cookie

steps.title: Set-Cookie carries the token
steps.spoken: Instead of returning the token in the body, the server sends it in a Set-Cookie response header. The browser sees that header and saves the cookie for this site.
steps.displayNarration: The server responds with a **`Set-Cookie`** header carrying `session=<token>`. The browser persists it scoped to the site.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — deliver the token via the Set-Cookie header

steps.title: The browser stores it
steps.spoken: The browser tucks the cookie away in its cookie jar, bound to this domain and path. From now on it belongs to the browser to manage.
steps.displayNarration: The browser stores the cookie under `Path=/` for the site's domain. It now owns delivery on every matching request.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — Path and domain scope the cookie

steps.title: Attached automatically
steps.spoken: Here is the magic that makes sessions feel seamless. On every later request to the site, the browser attaches the cookie all by itself, so the token travels without any application code.
steps.displayNarration: On each request to the origin, the browser auto-attaches the cookie in the **`Cookie`** header — no client code required.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — the browser sends the cookie on every request

steps.title: HttpOnly hides it from scripts
steps.spoken: That automatic sending is also a risk, so the cookie is hardened. HttpOnly means page scripts cannot read the cookie at all, so a cross-site scripting bug cannot simply steal the token.
steps.displayNarration: The cookie is set **`HttpOnly`**: JavaScript can't read `document.cookie` for it, so an XSS flaw can't exfiltrate the token directly.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — set HttpOnly to block script access

steps.title: SameSite blocks cross-site
steps.spoken: A malicious page on another domain might try to trigger a request to our site, hoping the browser attaches the cookie. SameSite, set to lax, tells the browser not to send the cookie on those cross-site requests, which blunts cross-site request forgery.
steps.displayNarration: **`SameSite=Lax`** stops the browser from attaching the cookie to cross-site requests a **malicious page** triggers — the core defense against CSRF.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — SameSite=Lax mitigates CSRF

steps.title: Secure and an expiry
steps.spoken: Two more attributes finish the job. Secure means the cookie only travels over an encrypted connection, never plaintext. And a max-age gives the cookie the same lifetime as the session itself.
steps.displayNarration: **`Secure`** restricts the cookie to HTTPS, and **`Max-Age`** matches the cookie's lifetime to the session's expiry.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — Secure and Max-Age attributes

steps.title: A token the browser carries
steps.spoken: The token now lives in a hardened cookie that the browser sends on every request and guards from scripts and other sites. Next, what the server does when that cookie arrives.
steps.displayNarration: The cookie is set once and **auto-sent** thereafter, locked down by `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, and `Secure`. Next: *validating* the token it carries.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/session-cookies — the hardened cookie travels on every request

chapters.title: Validating the Session
chapters.blurb: Every request rehashes the token, looks up the row by session ID, and checks it hasn't expired.

steps.title: Validating the Session
steps.coverSubtitle: The cookie arrives. Is this token real, whose is it, and is it still alive?
steps.spoken: A request arrives carrying the token. The server has to decide, quickly, whether to trust it.
steps.displayNarration: On each protected request the server **validates** the session token: recompute its ID, find the row, and check expiry.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — validate the session token on every request

steps.title: The token arrives
steps.spoken: A request comes in with the session cookie attached. The server pulls the raw token out of that cookie to begin validation.
steps.displayNarration: The server reads the **token** from the incoming `Cookie` header. It holds only the hash, so it can't use the token as-is.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — read the token from the request

steps.title: Recompute the session ID
steps.spoken: The server hashes the incoming token with the same one-way function used at creation. The same token always yields the same session ID, so this recomputes the database key without ever storing the token.
steps.displayNarration: Apply the same `SHA-256(token)` used at creation to recompute the **session ID** — the lookup key — deterministically.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — hash the token to recompute the session id

steps.title: Look up by session ID
steps.spoken: Using that session ID, the server queries the session store for a matching row. If no row exists, the token is forged or already deleted, and the request is rejected as unauthenticated.
steps.displayNarration: Query the store by `id = sessionId`. **No row** means the session is invalid — reject the request.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — look up the session by its id; missing means invalid

steps.title: The row names the user
steps.spoken: When a row is found, it carries the user identifier this session belongs to and the timestamp at which it expires. That is everything the server needs to know who is calling.
steps.displayNarration: The **session row** holds `user_id` and `expires_at`. The `user_id` is how the request learns *who* is making it.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — the row stores the user id and expiration

steps.title: Check expiration
steps.spoken: But a found row is not automatically valid. The server compares the expiry timestamp against the current time. If the session has expired, it deletes the row and rejects the request, just as if no session existed.
steps.displayNarration: Compare `expires_at` to *now*. If expired, **delete the row** and treat the request as unauthenticated.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — reject and delete expired sessions

steps.title: Run as that user
steps.spoken: If the row exists and has not expired, validation succeeds. The request now runs as that user, with no password and no second round trip required.
steps.displayNarration: A present, unexpired row means **success**: the request proceeds as `user_id`, authenticated by the token alone.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — a valid session authenticates the request

steps.title: Hash, find, check
steps.spoken: Validation is three steps: hash the token to an identifier, find the row, and confirm it is still alive. Last, what keeps a session fresh, and what ends it.
steps.displayNarration: Validation = **rehash → lookup → expiry check**. Next: sliding expiration and revocation — how a session stays alive or dies.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — validation recomputes, looks up, and checks expiry

chapters.title: Expiration and Revocation
chapters.blurb: Active sessions slide forward, idle ones expire, and logout deletes the row server-side.

steps.title: Expiration and Revocation
steps.coverSubtitle: A session shouldn't last forever, log active users out, or be impossible to kill.
steps.spoken: A good session expires on its own, stays out of an active user's way, and can be revoked at will.
steps.displayNarration: The final piece: managing a session's **lifetime** — sliding it forward for active users, expiring idle ones, and revoking on logout.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — session expiration and invalidation

steps.title: Check time left on each request
steps.spoken: On a valid request, the server looks at how much time is left before this session expires. That number decides whether anything needs to change.
steps.displayNarration: During validation the server reads `expires_at` and computes the **time remaining** before this session lapses.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — inspect remaining lifetime during validation

steps.title: Slide active sessions forward
steps.spoken: If less than half the lifetime remains, roughly fifteen days in, the server pushes the expiry another thirty days into the future. Active users are silently kept signed in without ever seeing a login screen.
steps.displayNarration: When under ~**15 days** remain, set `expires_at` ~30 days ahead again. This **sliding window** keeps active users logged in seamlessly.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — extend expiration when the session is past its halfway point

steps.title: Idle sessions just expire
steps.spoken: If the user walks away and stops making requests, nothing slides the expiry forward. Once the timestamp passes, the next validation deletes the row and the session is simply gone.
steps.displayNarration: With no requests, `expires_at` is never extended. After it passes, the next validation **deletes** the row — the session expires on its own.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — idle sessions lapse after the expiration window

steps.title: Logout deletes the row
steps.spoken: When the user logs out, the server deletes the session row outright and clears the cookie by sending an empty one that expires immediately. The token still exists in the wild, but it now points at nothing.
steps.displayNarration: Logout **deletes the row** server-side and sends a `Set-Cookie` with `Max-Age=0` to clear it. A leaked token now resolves to no session.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — invalidate a session by deleting it and clearing the cookie

steps.title: Revoke anywhere, instantly
steps.spoken: Because every session is just a row, the server holds real power. It can delete one device's session, or every session for a user at once, and the change takes effect on the very next request.
steps.displayNarration: Sessions are **server-side rows**, so you can revoke one or *all* of a user's sessions instantly — unlike a self-contained token you can't recall.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — server-side sessions can be revoked at any time

steps.title: The whole life of a session
steps.spoken: And that is the full journey. A sign-in mints a random token; its hash is stored as a row; the token rides home in a hardened cookie; every request rehashes it, finds the row, and checks expiry; active sessions slide forward while idle ones expire; and logout deletes the row for good.
steps.displayNarration: End to end: **mint → cookie → validate → slide or expire → revoke**. The token lives with the client; the authority always stays with the server.
sourceRefs: https://auth.pilcrowonpaper.com/sessions — the end-to-end session lifecycle
